ex-E303-1.title: Rate of heat transfer by conduction
ex-E303-1.question: An air conditioned room has a concrete wall facing outside. The wall is 10 cm thick and has an area of 9 m2. The temperatures of the inner and the outer surfaces of the wall are 25 °C and 33 °C respectively. The thermal conductivity of the concrete is 1.10 W m–1 K–1. Find the rate of heat transfer by conduction through the wall.
ex-E303-1.location: Book E3  |  Chapter E303  |  Source PDF p. 4

ex-E303-2.title: Rate of heat transfer and U-value
ex-E303-2.question:
(a) The size of an insulating wall is

6 m × 3 m. The temperatures of the two surfaces of the wall are 31 °C and 23 °C respectively. What is the rate of heat transfer through the wall? The U-value of the wall is 0.61 W m–2 K–1.

(b) If the wall is replaced by another wall of the same size, but with a higher U-value, how will the rate of heat transfer through the wall change?
ex-E303-2.answer:
(a) Area of the wall = 6 × 3

= 18 m2

Rate of heat transfer = UA(TH − TC)

= 0.61 × 18 × (31 − 23)

= 87.8 W

(b) Increase

ex-E303-3.title: U-value of a composite wall
ex-E303-3.question:
A wall is composed of a concrete layer and a wood fibre layer. They have different thicknesses and there is no air gap between them. The two sides of the wall are maintained at 32 °C and 25 °C respectively.

Given:

U-value of the concrete layer = 5.5 W m–2 K–1

U-value of the wood fibre layer = 0.95 W m–2 K–1

(a) Find the U-value of the wall.

(b) Find the temperature at the junction of the two layers.
ex-E303-3.answer:
(a) The temperature change across the whole wall equals the sum of the temperature changes across the two layers.

ΔT = ΔTc + ΔTw ................ (1)

The rate of heat transfer through each layer and through the whole wall should be the same. Let the rate be r.

For the whole wall: r = UAΔT ⇒ ΔT = rUA

For the concrete layer: r = Uc AΔTc ⇒ ΔTc = rUcA

For the wood fibre layer: r = UwAΔTw ⇒ ΔTw = rUwA

Therefore, (1) becomes:

rUA = rUcA + rUwA

1U = 1Uc + 1Uw

= 15.5 + 10.95

U = 0.810 W m–2 K–1

(b) Let Tj be the temperature at the junction of the two layers.

Rate of heat transfer in concrete = rate of heat transfer in wood fibre

UcAcΔTc = UwAwΔTw

(5.5)(A)(32 − Tj) = (0.95)(A)(Tj − 25)

Tj = 31.0 °C
ex-E303-3.location: Book E3  |  Chapter E303  |  Source PDF p. 8

ex-E303-4.title: Total rate of heat transfer by conduction through a wall with windows
ex-E303-4.question:
One side of the wall in the building shown is 50 m wide and 170 m tall. On the wall, there are 552 identical windows, each of area 8.7 m2. If the temperature difference between the interior and the exterior of the building is 8 °C, find the total rate of heat transfer by conduction through the wall with windows.

Given that the U-values of the window and the wall are 2.8 W m–2 K–1 and 4.2 W m–2 K–1 respectively.
ex-E303-4.answer:
Apply Qt = UA(TH − TC).

Rate of heat transfer by conduction through all windows

= 2.8 × (552 × 8.7) × 8 = 108 000 W

Rate of heat transfer by conduction through the wall (excluding windows)

= 4.2 × (50 × 170 – 552 × 8.7) × 8 = 124 000 W

Total rate of heat transfer by conduction through the wall with windows

= 108 000 + 124 000 = 232 000 W
ex-E303-4.location: Book E3  |  Chapter E303  |  Source PDF p. 9

ex-E303-5.title: Radiation through different windows
ex-E303-5.question:
John sets up an experiment to record the temperature rise inside a box. The box has an opening for fitting a window. When it is fitted tightly with a window, the box is completely enclosed.

John first attaches a single-glazed window and then a double-glazed window to the opening. He finds that although the double-glazed window has a lower U-value, the rise in temperature in both cases is almost the same. Give an explanation for this result.
ex-E303-5.answer: The U-value is related to heat transfer by conduction. In the experiment, heat is transferred through the windows predominantly by radiation. The amount of radiation passing through both windows is about the same. Therefore, the rise in temperature in both cases is almost the same.
ex-E303-5.location: Book E3  |  Chapter E303  |  Source PDF p. 10

ex-E303-6.title: OTTV of a building
ex-E303-6.question:
A building has four walls and a roof. There are some double-glazed windows on the walls. The total area of the windows is 700 m2. The table shows the properties of the walls and the roof.

Walls (excluding windows)

Roof

Total area / m2

4000

U-value / W m−2 K−1

(a) The equivalent temperature difference between the interior and the exterior of the building is 5 °C. Find the total rate of heat gain through the walls and the roof.

(b) The rate of heat gain per unit area through the windows is 130 W m–2. Find the total rate of heat gain through the windows.

(c) Find the OTTV of the building.
ex-E303-6.answer:
(a) By Qt = UA(TH − TC),

total rate of heat gain through walls and roof

ex-E303-7.title: Charging a battery pack of an electric vehicle
ex-E303-7.question: An electric vehicle uses a battery pack of capacity 24 kW h. The driver wants to charge the battery pack from 0% to 80% of its full capacity. If a medium charger is used, the battery pack will be charged with a terminal voltage of 220 V and an average current of 32 A. How long will the charging process take? Assume no energy is lost during the charging process.
ex-E303-7.tips:
Tip

In equation E = VIt, if E is

measured in W h, the unit of t should be h.
ex-E303-7.location: Book E3  |  Chapter E303  |  Source PDF p. 25

ex-E303-8.title: Battery capacity and range of an electric vehicle
ex-E303-8.question:
An electric vehicle uses a battery pack of capacity 60 kW h. The power consumption of the vehicle motor is 4 kW when the vehicle moves at a constant speed of 30 km h−1.

(a) Due to the energy loss from the electric circuit, the total energy supplied to the motor is only 85% of the energy stored in the battery. Estimate the range of the vehicle under this mode of driving.

(b) What is most of the energy output of the motor used for?
ex-E303-8.answer:
(a) Total energy output of motor = 60 × 85% = 51 kW h

By E = Pt,

time for consuming all the energy = EP = 514 = 12.75 h

Range of the vehicle = vt = 30 × 12.75 = 383 km

(b) Most of the energy output of the motor is used to overcome friction and air resistance.
ex-E303-8.location: Book E3  |  Chapter E303  |  Source PDF p. 26

ex-E303-9.title: Running costs of cars
ex-E303-9.question:
A customer is choosing between a fossil-fuel car and an electric car.

(a) Suggest two reasons why an electric vehicle is more energy efficient than a fossil-fuel vehicle of similar size.

(b) The fuel consumption of the fossil-fuel car is 7.8 L per 100 km while the power consumption of the electric car is 14.3 kW h per 100 km. Each litre of fuel costs $15 while each kW h of electricity costs $2.9. Suppose the car has to runs an average of 60 km a day. What is the cost of fuel/electricity used by each car each day?
ex-E303-9.answer:
(a) An electric motor is more efficient than a combustion engine in terms of energy conversion.

An electric vehicle has a regenerative braking system which can convert the kinetic energy of the vehicle back into chemical energy in the battery for future use during braking.

(b) Fuel used by the fossil-fuel car each day

= 7.8 × 60100 = 4.68 L

Cost of fuel used each day

= 15 × 4.68 = $70.2

Electricity used by the electric car each day

= 14.3 × 60100 = 8.58 kW h

Cost of electricity used each day

= 2.9 × 8.58 = $24.9

Exercise 3.2 Q9 (p.120)
ex-E303-9.location: Book E3  |  Chapter E303  |  Source PDF p. 28

ex-E303-10.title: Charging battery directly by engine
ex-E303-10.question:
In some types of hybrid vehicles, the combustion engine can propel the vehicle and charge the battery at the same time when the travelling speed is low.

(a) Explain why these vehicles can charge their batteries when their speeds are low.

(b) State the energy conversions for the charging process briefly.
ex-E303-10.answer:
(a) When the vehicle travels at a low speed, the power output required is low. The engine can then provide excess power to charge the battery.

(b) Chemical energy in petrol

→ KE of generator

→ electrical energy

→ chemical energy in battery
ex-E303-10.location: Book E3  |  Chapter E303  |  Source PDF p. 30

ex-E303-11.title: Energy consumed by buses and cars
ex-E303-11.question:
In Hong Kong, about 3 million passengers travel by bus every day. Suppose that all these passengers travelled by taxi instead of bus.

(a) How much more energy would be used due to these passengers per kilometre of travel? The amount of energy needed per person per kilometre for buses and taxis is about 1.5 × 106 J and 2.9 × 106 J respectively.

(b) How much more carbon dioxide would be emitted due to these passengers per kilometre of travel? The amount of carbon dioxide emission associated with a person per kilometre for buses and taxis is 38 g and 120 g respectively.
ex-E303-11.answer:
(a) Additional amount of energy used per km

= (2.9 − 1.5) × 106 × 3 × 106 = 4.2 × 1012 J

(b) Additional amount of carbon dioxide emitted per km

= (120 – 38) × 3 × 106 = 2.46 × 108 g = 2.46 × 105 kg
ex-E303-11.location: Book E3  |  Chapter E303  |  Source PDF p. 35
